Mexico City, Aug. 5.— How Matthew Gourd, an American
farmer, was lashed to a tree and forced to witness an attack on his
two daughters by bandits, is a story brought here today from
Tampico.
The person relating the story said the bandits first requested
a cigarette from Gourd, who complied, and a peso was offered in
payment for them. Gourd was then tied and with a knife at his
throat was ordered to produce his money. He told his seventeen-
year-old daughter to bring the money from the house, and on her
appearance she was seized and together with her sister aged thir
teen years, was mistreated. When the rebels left the women un
tied the father, who reported the assault to the authorities at Tam
pico. One version of the affair is that the assailants were not rebels,
but peons employed on Gourd's own farm near the Atascador
colony.

Washington, Aug. 5.—That no an
nouncement of policy or further
steps will be taken by President Wfl-
son in the Mexican situation until
former Governor John Lynd, of Min
nesota, personal representative of
the President, arrives in Mexico City
and familiarizes himself with condi
tions there, was made clear at the
White House today.
Mr. Lynd carries instructions to
talk informally with prominent Mexi
cans. Washington officials indicated
that no steps toward a mediation
policy would be attempted until after
Mr. Lynd had sounded out senti-
ment in Mexico, and determined
whether the assistance of the Unit
ed States in adjusting the dispute will
be received.
Mr. Lynd will inform inquirers on
the authority of President Wilson
that only a government constitution
ally set up would be recognized by
the United States. This will involve
the resignation of Provisional Presi
dent Huerta in favor of the previous
president selected by the Mexican
factions. The new president to be
first appointed minister of foreign re
lations in conformity with the law cf
cussession in Mexico.
It was pointed out in administra
tion circles today, that while Mr.
Lynd 's position now is that of adviser
to the American Embassy, he will
act in reality as an ambassador, to
be named ambassador when a stable
government is organized and recog
nition is extended by the United
States.
Disappointment in Mexico.
Mexico City, Aug. 5—The news of
the dismissal of Henry Lane Wilson,
the American Ambassador, and the
appointment by President Wilson of
ex-Governor Lind, of Minnesota, to
come to Mexico as a special peace
emissary has caused keen disappoint
ment and a good deal of apprehension
amongst Americans and also amongst
Mexicans here. Strong belief here
prevails that the course of action tak
en by the United States administra
tion is unwise, and so far from recon
ciling opposing factions the more pro
bable result will be to make the exist
ing confusion worse confounded.
General Huerta has emphatically de
clared that he will neither resign nor
accept mediation, and it is feared that
President Wilson's peace emissary
will make little or no impression upon
him until the United States makes for
mal recognition of his government.

London, Aug 5.—The Washington
reports of Great Britain's intention to
establish a great naval base at Ber-
muda are regarded here as a gross
exaggeration and misconception of
the Admiralty’s plans relative to the
naval utiliatizon of the island.
It is admitted that the Admiralty
is taking measures to increase the
Brit’sh squadron in those waters and
to develop Bermuda as a dockyard
and coaling station, but it is declared
that this is merely to remedy a mis
take that was made under Admiral
Fisher’s regime.
Bermuda, it is argued, has been a
British possession since 1609, long
before the Monroe doctrine existed,
and it became a regular coaling sta L
tion in 1869, and was made the
headquarters of the North American
and West Indies squadron years ago.
Under Lord Fisher's naval redistri-
bution scheme, owing to the naval
pressure in Europe, the number of
ships that had headquarters at Ber-
muda was reduced, but the dockyard
was always maintained .
So far as is known, all that the Ad
miralty now intends to do is to sta
tion four armored cruisers in the
West Indies during the winter
months. No battleships are going
there.
Receipts Pouring in Rapidly Under the New Crown

—The Government Meeting.
Attorney General Grimmer, who has
not been enjoying very good health for
some time, is here from St. Stephen
for the meeting of the Government
and the other ministers are expected
to arrive this evening. A number of
members of the Legislative Assembly
are here including Mr. Woods, of
Queens, and Messrs. Culligan and
Stewart of Restigouche. The latter
report an unusually prosperous season
on the North Shore with the best out-
look for the crops in years and the
roads in better shape than ever be
fore. The lumber industry is also en
joying a prosperous season, the sales
having been made in the spring when
prices were much higher than at pres
ent.
The first session of the executive
council will be held this evening and to-
morrow it is expected that a meeting
of the Board of Education will be
held.
At the Crown Land Department to-
day announcement was made that the
receipts from bonuses, stumpage
and mileage renewals to date amount
to about $425,000. Of the total about
$150,000 is in bonuses for licenses is
sued under the new Crown Timber
Lands Act.
Premier Flemming, who arrived last
evening from Woodstock for the meet-
ing of the Provincial Government
which opens this evening, expressed
himself as much pleased with the sat
isfactory manner in which the provis
ions of the new act were being worked
out. About all the big limit holders
have come in under the provisions of
the new act and are taking out the
new licenses while those continuing
under the old licenses will be only a
few small holders who in the aggre
gate hold a comparatively small area
under license.

London, Aug. 5—Premier Asquith
presided at the opening session of the
annual conference of the national as
sociation for the prevention of tuber-
culosis. Dr. H. W. H. MacKenzie, phy
sician at the Brompton Hospital for
consumption, making a general survey
of the results of the tubercular treat-
ment, said it was not to be maintain
ed that the cures had been a success.
Antagonistic germs in the body, he
said, militated against it. The treat
ment is still on trial, Dr. MacKenzie
said, but it must be acknowledged
that the results so far have been far
from brilliant and are unconvincing.

Paris, Aug. 5.--The chief physisian
of the Vila Juna insane asylum an
nounces that infections of oxygen
made by him cured in a few days two
cases of an acute type of sudden
madness. He believes the treatment
will always be efficacious in madness

Chicago, Ill., Aug. 5—Chicago's ten
police women, clad in modest blue
bands, went on duty today. Their
work will be mainly to look out for wo
men and children. The details of
their duties, apparel and powers, have
been worked out by a committee of
women social workers and the chief of
police. The chief had considered as
signing the police women to stations
in the red light districts, but it was
decided they would be of greater ser
vice in the parks and other places of
recreation.
The police women will visit the pub
lic dance halls, excursion boats, beach
es and railway stations, and will try
to keep young folks off the streets
late at night. They will obtain infor
mation rather than make arrests, al
though on occasions they may be call
ed upon to arres some one.
Whether the police women shall
wear brass buttons and carry revol
vers and clubs will be decided after
the civil service examination for the
position.

London, Aug. 5.—Although the Mo
ther Country has refused to partici
pate in the Panama Canal Exposi-
tion, Australia intends to be repre-
sented.
The Morning Post's correspondent
at Sydney, N. S. W., says the Com
monwealth Government has guaran
teed £20,000, and New South Wales,
Queensland and Victoria have agreed
to co-operate in a joint exhibit. Trad
ers here are convinced that a grow
ing market in the United States
will be assisted by the opening of the
Panama Canal and the reduction of
the United States customs duties
foreshadowed in the new tariff bill.
Hon. Mr. Glynn, Minister for Ex
ternal Affairs, has sketched out an
extensive scheme for the advertising
of Australia in the United States,
and the appointment of a number of
commercial agents in the various
places there.

Philadelphia, Aug. 5.—The Blue
Mountain House at Pen-Mar, on the
Pennsylvania and Hartland, was de
stroyed by fire today. Two guests,
B. F. Metzgar and Malcolm Frank, of

were driven to the lawns in scanty
attire, few being able to save their
belongings.

ago, and in its day was one of the
best known mountain resort houses

London, Aug. 5.—C. N. Armstrong,
of Montreal, who is the Conservative
candidate for Colno Valley, declares
he would not object to Ireland having
the same kind of Home Rule as Can
ada has. He would have such a sys
tem applicable to Scotland and Wales,
as the House of Commons had too
much in hand already to attend to
trifling local matters. He added, there
is too much blind party following at
Westminster, and he wants to repre
sent those who are opposed as well
as those voting for him.

Calgary, Alta., Aug. 5.—Fred Star-

Florence, Aug. F.—Jewelry to the
value of $3,200 was stolen yesterday
from the apartment of Miss Blood, an
American resident of Florence, who is
a friend of Princess Chica, sister of
formen Queen Natalie of Servia. She
had rented the Villa Gamberal, the
home of the Princess, for the season.
The apartment was ransacked in the
absence of Miss Blood and the safe
opened, the key having been obtained
by the thieves by means of a forged
letter. The fact that a band was con-
nected in the robbery was shown
when a letter telling of the plot was
found in the apartment.

Rundschau says that a special cruiser

look after German interests abroad.

to be formed into a flying squadron.
